title: Language Access, Accessibility, and De-escalation

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe language access services and the appropriate use of qualified interpreters.
- Identify accessibility accommodations for patients with disabilities.
- Apply de-escalation techniques to calm and safely assist upset patients.
- Demonstrate respectful, non-judgmental communication with all patients.
- Protect patient privacy and confidentiality during every communication.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Imagine trying to follow a recipe written in a language you barely know; you might miss important steps. LEP means a patient has trouble with English the same way, so they need extra help to understand their care.

### Question 2

Just like a store must provide a ramp for a wheelchair, a medical office must provide language help so every patient can understand. It should not make the patient pay or bring their own helper.

### Question 3

If someone came to your lemonade stand speaking another language, the helpful thing is to find a translator, not to yell or send them home. You first find out what language they speak, then get help.

### Question 4

Think of an interpreter like a professional translator at an important meeting; you want someone trained to be accurate and keep secrets, not just anyone who knows both languages.

### Question 5

Imagine asking a kid to explain a grown-up's serious health problem; they might not know the words, and it is too much pressure for them. Grown-up translators should do this job.

### Question 6

Even if a family member speaks both languages, a doctor's office should offer its own professional translator, like using an official referee instead of a friend who might take sides or miss things.

### Question 7

When you talk through a translator, you still look at and talk to the person you are really speaking with, just like talking to a friend even when a translator repeats your words.

### Question 8

Think of a triangle where everyone can see each other's faces, like friends sitting around a table so no one is left out of the talk.

### Question 9

It is like passing a bucket of water one cup at a time instead of dumping the whole bucket at once; small pieces are easier to carry without spilling.

### Question 10

An ad hoc interpreter is like grabbing any random person in the room to translate, instead of calling a trained professional.

### Question 11

It is like writing down that a customer prefers to be helped in a certain way, so the whole team remembers and prepares next time.

### Question 12

It is like calling a special hotline where a trained translator joins your phone call and helps two people who speak different languages talk to each other.

### Question 13

Video interpreting is like a video call with a translator who can see you, which matters when people talk with their hands or faces.

### Question 14

If someone talks with their hands instead of their voice, the best help is a professional who knows that hand language, not shouting.

### Question 15

Knowing two languages is not the same as being trained to translate medical talk, just like knowing how to swim is not the same as being a lifeguard.

### Question 16

A translator is like a vault; whatever they hear during a private medical talk stays locked up and is not shared with others.

### Question 17

If a person politely says they would rather have their brother translate, you can let them choose but still offer your professional translator and make sure they really understand.

### Question 18

Consecutive is like waiting for someone to finish a sentence before you tell your friend; simultaneous is like a live voice-over that happens while the person is still talking.

### Question 19

Before a big relay race, you tell each runner the plan; briefing the translator is the same so everyone knows the goal and the rules.

### Question 20

The translator pretends to be the voice of each person, saying exactly what they said, like passing a note word for word instead of your own version.

### Question 21

It is hard to repeat a very long, confusing sentence exactly; breaking it into small, clear pieces makes the translation right.

### Question 22

Health literacy is about understanding doctor instructions, not just knowing English. A person can speak English perfectly and still be confused by big medical words.

### Question 23

If many customers read a different language, a good store prints its signs and forms in that language too, so everyone can understand.

### Question 24

A TTY is like a texting phone that lets people who cannot hear or speak easily still make phone calls with help.

### Question 25

Instead of trusting a nod, ask the person to say the steps back in their own words, like checking that someone can repeat a recipe before they cook alone.

### Question 26

It is like booking a translator before a meeting so everything is ready when the person walks in.

### Question 27

If the translator is busy and it is not an emergency, the smart move is to plan the talk for later when the translator is free.

### Question 28

In an emergency, getting help right away comes first, like calling for help when someone is hurt even if you cannot perfectly explain everything.

### Question 29

This law is like a promise that public places, including doctors' offices, must be usable by everyone, with ramps and other help as needed.

### Question 30

A reasonable accommodation is a fair change, like moving a shelf lower, that lets someone use a service without causing big problems for the business.

### Question 31

These are tools like translators, big-print papers, and special hearing devices that help people understand and be understood.

### Question 32

If someone uses a wheelchair, you make sure the way is clear and ask how you can help, instead of grabbing them or taking their chair.

### Question 33

If someone cannot read small print, you can read the questions to them or give them a big-print copy, so they can answer for themselves.

### Question 34

If someone prefers to write notes back and forth, you do that, because they know the best way to communicate.

### Question 35

To help someone who cannot hear well, look at them, turn down the noise, and talk clearly so they can see your face and lips.

### Question 36

A service animal is like a trained assistant with a real job, while an emotional support animal is more like a comforting pet without special training.

### Question 37

A good exam room has a table that lowers, a door wide enough for a wheelchair, and sturdy bars to hold onto.

### Question 38

You talk to the person themselves with kind, simple words, and let their helper join in when needed, just like including a friend who brings along a buddy.

### Question 39

A cane is like a person's steady helper; you let them keep using it and only help if they ask.

### Question 40

If a door has steps and no ramp, the right move is to tell the boss and find another safe way in, not to ignore it or try to carry the person.

### Question 41

It means giving the right tools, like a sign-language translator, for free, so the person understands everything just like a hearing person would.

### Question 42

Ask the person what works best for them, like asking which game a friend wants to play instead of picking your favorite.

### Question 43

It is like a special microphone that makes the speaker's voice louder and the room quieter, so someone who cannot hear well can follow along.

### Question 44

Braille and big letters let people who cannot see regular print still read the signs and papers, like adding a sound to a picture.

### Question 45

A video doctor visit needs captions or a translator too, so everyone can see and understand what is said.

### Question 46

Whether a person needs help for a short time or always, the office should still make things work for them.

### Question 47

Some health problems cannot be seen, like a heart or lung condition, so you cannot tell just by looking whether someone needs the closer space.

### Question 48

Accessible parking is like saving the closest, easiest spots for people who have a harder time walking.

### Question 49

If a request is above your level, you pass it to the person in charge, like asking a manager when you cannot solve a customer's problem yourself.

### Question 50

Moving someone safely is a team job with the right tools, like using two people and a ramp instead of one person trying to lift something heavy alone.

### Question 51

If someone talks using a special machine, you wait patiently and listen, just like waiting for anyone to finish their sentence.

### Question 52

Some people read with a computer that speaks the words aloud, so giving them a digital form instead of paper is just making it readable for them.

### Question 53

The doctor's office pays for the translator, just like it pays for the ramp, so the patient does not have to.

### Question 54

Practice and learning help the whole team remember how to welcome and help every person, like rehearsing before a show.

### Question 55

When someone is upset, staying calm and listening is like adding cool water to a hot pan instead of more heat.

### Question 56

Active listening is like catching what someone says, saying it back to be sure, and really paying attention instead of just waiting for your turn.

### Question 57

A soft, steady voice is like a gentle hand on a nervous animal; it helps everyone calm down.

### Question 58

If someone is yelling and you talk quietly, they often quiet down to hear you, like turning down music to hear a whisper.

### Question 59

Saying 'I get why you are upset, let me help' is like telling a friend you understand their problem and then fixing it together.

### Question 60

When someone is upset, giving them a little room is like giving a cat space to calm down instead of cornering it.

### Question 61

First listen, then calmly share the true facts, like a referee who hears both sides before explaining what really happened.

### Question 62

If a mix-up happens, letting the person pick between two good options is like offering them a choice of desserts after a mistake, which makes them feel better.

### Question 63

It is okay to say 'I want to help, but please do not call me names,' like a coach who sets fair rules while still wanting to play the game.

### Question 64

If you feel unsafe, your first job is to get help and get somewhere safe, just like calling for a grown-up when a situation feels dangerous.

### Question 65

It is like sitting near the door at a movie theater so you can leave easily if you need to, and knowing where the fire exit is.

### Question 66

Moving a loud, upset conversation to a quiet private room is like taking a personal chat somewhere no one else can hear.

### Question 67

Saying 'calm down, it is no big deal' is like pouring gasoline on a small fire; it usually makes the person more upset, not less.

### Question 68

Open arms and a friendly face say 'I am here to help,' like welcoming someone with a smile instead of a scowl.

### Question 69

After a hard moment, writing down exactly what happened and telling the boss is like making a note in a class log so everyone stays safe and informed.

### Question 70

If someone says they are going to hurt someone, you stop and get help right away, like pulling a fire alarm instead of trying to put out a big fire alone.

### Question 71

It is like saying 'a girl who has a cast' instead of 'the broken-arm girl,' because the person comes first, not the injury.

### Question 72

Calling someone 'bad at following directions' is mean and misses the real story; saying what actually happened is fair and useful.

### Question 73

Instead of scolding, say thank you and offer to help, like a friend who says 'thanks for telling me, let's figure this out.'

### Question 74

Asking 'tell me more about it' is like opening a door wide, while a yes-or-no question only opens it a tiny crack.

### Question 75

If someone says 'please call me by this name,' you use that name, just like calling a friend by the nickname they prefer.

### Question 76

Explain things in simple words, like describing a game's rules without using confusing expert terms.

### Question 77

Ask the person to tell the steps back to you, like having a student repeat the homework directions so you know they got it.

### Question 78

Every person is different, so the polite thing is to notice how someone likes to communicate and meet them there, like matching a friend's pace instead of guessing from where they are from.

### Question 79

Talking quietly at the front desk is like whispering a secret so no one else hears your private business.

### Question 80

If a friend starts sharing something private in a crowded room, you move to a quiet corner, because some things are just for the two of you.

### Question 81

Talk to the person whose appointment it is, and let them decide how much their companion helps, like asking the birthday child what they want instead of their parent.

### Question 82

When you realize you got something wrong about a friend, you change what you are doing and treat them right, instead of pretending nothing happened.

### Question 83

When people feel listened to and respected, they trust you more and tell you the important stuff, like a friend who opens up because you are kind.
